author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Determine that the thing can and shall be done, and then we shall find the way.
work: Speech in the House of Representatives (20 June 1848)
significance: Big tasks yield to firm resolve; once you commit that something must happen, practical paths tend to appear.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing.
significance: Talent and circumstance matter, but your own steady determination is the factor most within your control.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: The leading rule for the lawyer, as for the man of every other calling, is diligence. Leave nothing for to-morrow which can be done to-day.
significance: Diligence is the common rule of every calling; doing today's work today keeps small tasks from becoming burdens.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Resolve to be honest at all events; and if in your own judgment you cannot be an honest lawyer, resolve to be honest without being a lawyer.
significance: Integrity comes before career; if a role would require dishonesty, it is the role that should go, not the honesty.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Let us have faith that right makes might, and in that faith, let us, to the end, dare to do our duty as we understand it.
significance: Doing right is not always easy or rewarded at once, yet leaders are asked to act on conviction and trust that right will hold.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Upon the subject of education, not presuming to dictate any plan or system respecting it, I can only say that I view it as the most important subject which we as a people can be engaged in.
work: Address to the People of Sangamon County (9 March 1832)
significance: Education shapes a people's future, which is why teaching remains one of the most important things a community does.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Far and away the best prize that life offers is the chance to work hard at work worth doing.
work: Labor Day Address, New York State Agricultural Association, Syracuse (7 September 1903)
significance: Meaningful, demanding work is a gift, not a burden; the chance to labour at something worthwhile is itself a reward.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is not the critic who counts, not the man who points out how the strong man stumbled, or where the doer of deeds could have done better.
significance: Critics are easy to find; credit belongs to those who step forward, try, and risk failure in doing real work.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: In short, in life, as in a football game, the principle to follow is: Hit the line hard; don't foul and don't shirk, but hit the line hard!
significance: Play fair and give full effort: no cheating and no slacking, but meet hard things head-on.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Be practical as well as generous in your ideals. Keep your eyes on the stars, but remember to keep your feet on the ground.
work: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
significance: Aim high, but stay practical; ideals only change things when they are joined to realistic, grounded action.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: I don't pity any man who does hard work worth doing. I admire him. I pity the creature who does not work, at whichever end of the social scale he may regard himself as being.
work: Remarks to the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, Chattanooga (8 September 1902)
significance: Honest labour of any kind deserves respect, while idleness diminishes a person whatever their wealth or status.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: We cannot avoid meeting great issues. All that we can determine for ourselves is whether we shall meet them well or ill.
significance: We do not get to choose all our challenges; we do choose whether to face them with courage and care.

author: George Washington
text: Be courteous to all, but intimate with few, and let those few be well tried before you give them your confidence; true friendship is a plant of slow growth.
significance: Be kind to everyone but careful with trust; deep friendships are tested slowly and are worth the wait.

author: George Washington
text: I hope I shall always possess firmness and virtue enough to maintain (what I consider the most enviable of all titles) the character of an honest man.
significance: A good reputation for honesty is worth more than any title or honour a leader could be given.

author: George Washington
text: It is better to offer no excuse than a bad one.
significance: A weak excuse damages trust more than a plain admission; owning a failure is the better path.

author: George Washington
text: Promote, then, as an object of primary importance, institutions for the general diffusion of knowledge.
significance: A free and healthy society depends on spreading knowledge widely, which makes schools and teachers vital.

author: George Washington
text: Discipline is the soul of an army. It makes small numbers formidable; procures success to the weak, and esteem to all.
work: Letter of Instructions to the Captains of the Virginia Regiments (29 July 1759)
significance: Order and self-control let a small, ordinary group achieve far more than its size would suggest.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Never give in — never, never, never, never, in nothing great or small, large or petty, never give in except to convictions of honour and good sense.
significance: Perseverance matters, but so does wisdom: hold firm on what matters while staying open to honour and good sense.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities, because, as has been said, it is the quality which guarantees all others.
work: "Unlucky Alfonso", Collier's (27 June 1931); reprinted in Great Contemporaries (1937)
significance: Without courage, other virtues fail under pressure; it is what lets honesty, kindness and loyalty hold when tested.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Personally, I am always ready to learn, although I do not always like being taught.
work: Speech in the House of Commons (4 November 1952)
significance: Even strong leaders find correction uncomfortable; the goal is to keep learning anyway.

author: Winston Churchill
text: To improve is to change, so to be perfect is to have changed often.
work: Speech in the House of Commons (23 June 1925)
significance: Growth requires change; those who improve most are willing to adjust again and again.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Every day you may make progress. Every step may be fruitful. Yet there will stretch out before you an ever-lengthening, ever-ascending, ever-improving path.
work: "Painting as a Pastime", The Strand Magazine (1921–22)
significance: Steady daily effort compounds; there is always further to grow, which keeps work and learning fresh.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Where my reason, imagination or interest were not engaged, I would not or I could not learn.
significance: Students learn best when their reason, imagination or interest is engaged, a reminder for every teacher and parent.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Resolution. Resolve to perform what you ought; perform without fail what you resolve.
work: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
significance: Make fewer promises to yourself, and keep the ones you make; character is built on follow-through.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Industry. Lose no time; be always employ'd in something useful; cut off all unnecessary actions.
work: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
significance: Time is a resource; using it on useful work and cutting waste makes room for what matters most.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Human felicity is produc'd not so much by great pieces of good fortune that seldom happen, as by little advantages that occur every day.
significance: Happiness is built more from small daily kindnesses and habits than from rare windfalls.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: From a child I was fond of reading, and all the little money that came into my hands was ever laid out in books.
significance: A love of reading formed in childhood can shape a whole life; books are a wise place to spend what we have.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: For my own Part, when I am employed in serving others, I do not look upon myself as conferring Favours, but as paying Debts.
significance: Serving others is not a favour we grant but a debt we owe for all we have received.

author: Peter Drucker
text: The purpose of an organization is to enable common men to do uncommon things.
significance: Good organisations let ordinary people achieve extraordinary results together, which is a test of any team or school.

author: Peter Drucker
text: A superior who works on his own development sets an almost irresistible example.
significance: Leaders who keep growing themselves set an example that shapes their teams more than any instruction.

author: Peter Drucker
text: A man should never be appointed into a managerial position if his vision focuses on people's weaknesses rather than on their strengths.
significance: Leaders should build on people's strengths; fixating on weaknesses drains a team and wastes talent.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Morale in an organization does not mean that "people get along together"; the test is performance not conformance.
significance: Good morale is not just getting along; it shows in whether a team does excellent work together.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Effective executives do first things first and they do one thing at a time.
work: The Effective Executive, ch. 5 "First Things First" (1966)
significance: Focus beats busyness: doing the most important thing first, one at a time, is how effective people get results.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: What counts is not necessarily the size of the dog in the fight — it's the size of the fight in the dog.
work: Remarks at Republican National Committee Breakfast (31 January 1958)
significance: Determination and heart often matter more than size or resources when facing a hard challenge.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Humility must always be the portion of any man who receives acclaim earned in blood of his followers and sacrifices of his friends.
significance: Leaders who receive praise should stay humble, remembering the sacrifices others made to earn it.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: The essence of leadership is to get others to do something because they think you want it done and because they know it is worth while doing.
work: Remarks at the Republican Campaign Picnic, Gettysburg Farm (12 September 1956)
significance: Real leadership persuades people that the work is worth doing, rather than simply giving orders.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Leadership consists of nothing but taking responsibility for everything that goes wrong and giving your subordinates credit for everything that goes well.
work: Interview in Edgar F. Puryear Jr., Nineteen Stars (1971)
significance: Good leaders take the blame when things go wrong and pass the credit to their team when things go well.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: Plans are worthless, but planning is everything.
work: Remarks at the National Defense Executive Reserve Conference (14 November 1957)
significance: Plans change once reality arrives, but the thinking done while planning prepares you to adapt well.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I learned the lesson that great men cultivate love, and that only little men cherish a spirit of hatred.
significance: Hatred shrinks the person who holds it; greatness of character shows in choosing love instead.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I would permit no man, no matter what his colour might be, to narrow and degrade my soul by making me hate him.
significance: Refusing to hate those who wrong us protects our own souls, even when bitterness would feel justified.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: Few things help an individual more than to place responsibility upon him, and to let him know that you trust him.
significance: Trusting people with real responsibility helps them grow; leaders and parents can give that gift.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I have learned that success is to be measured not so much by the position that one has reached in life as by the obstacles which he has overcome while trying to succeed.
significance: Success is measured not only by where we end up but by the obstacles we overcome on the way.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: Nothing ever comes to me, that is worth having, except as the result of hard work.
significance: Worthwhile things rarely come easily; steady hard work is usually the price of what is worth having.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: In meeting men, in many places, I have found that the happiest people are those who do the most for others; the most miserable are those who do the least.
significance: Joy is closely tied to service; those who give most to others often find the deepest happiness.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: If there is no struggle, there is no progress. Those who profess to favor freedom, and yet depreciate agitation, are men who want crops without plowing up the ground.
work: West India Emancipation speech, Canandaigua, New York (August 1857)
significance: Real progress requires struggle; wanting good results without hard effort is like wanting a harvest without ploughing.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: I would unite with anybody to do right; and with nobody to do wrong.
significance: Work with anyone for a good cause, but never join anyone in doing wrong; cooperation has a moral limit.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: You have seen how a man was made a slave; you shall see how a slave was made a man.
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 10 (1845)
significance: Courage and learning can restore a person's dignity, turning a story of oppression into one of freedom.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 6 (1845)
significance: For Douglass, learning to read opened the way to freedom, a reminder of how much education can change a life.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: My theory of self-made men is, then, simply this: that they are men of work.
work: Self-Made Men, address at Carlisle Indian Industrial School (c. 1893)
significance: Behind most success lies plain, persistent work rather than luck or genius, which is encouraging for everyone.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: Nothing valuable can be lost by taking time.
significance: Under pressure, a pause to think rarely costs anything good, while haste can cost a great deal.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: The dogmas of the quiet past are inadequate to the stormy present. The occasion is piled high with difficulty, and we must rise with the occasion.
significance: Old habits may not fit new challenges; leaders must be willing to think freshly when circumstances change.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: In this sad world of ours, sorrow comes to all; and, to the young, it comes with bitterest agony, because it takes them unawares.
significance: Written to a grieving girl, it models gentle honesty about grief, especially for children meeting loss for the first time.

author: Abraham Lincoln
text: I shall try to correct errors when shown to be errors; and I shall adopt new views so fast as they shall appear to be true views.
significance: Admitting mistakes and updating your views is a strength in a leader, not a weakness.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: A sound body is good; a sound mind is better; but a strong and clean character is better than either.
work: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
significance: Health and intellect matter, but character is what most deserves our effort as learners, parents and teachers.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: Happiness can not come to any man capable of enjoying true happiness unless it comes as the sequel to duty well and honestly done.
work: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
significance: Lasting contentment tends to follow faithful work and kept responsibilities rather than the chase for pleasure.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: The same qualities that make a decent boy make a decent man. They have different manifestations, but fundamentally they are the same.
work: Address at Prize Day, Groton School (24 May 1904)
significance: The habits children practise now are the character they will carry as adults, which is why small lessons matter.

author: Theodore Roosevelt
text: It is hard to fail, but it is worse never to have tried to succeed. In this life we get nothing save by effort.
work: The Strenuous Life, speech to the Hamilton Club, Chicago (10 April 1899)
significance: Failure hurts, but never trying costs more; growth comes only through effort that risks falling short.

author: George Washington
text: A slender acquaintance with the world must convince every man, that actions, not words, are the true criterion of the attachment of his friends
work: Letter to Major-General John Sullivan (15 December 1779)
significance: Loyalty shows in what people do, not what they say, and the same test applies to our own commitments.

author: George Washington
text: Of all the dispositions and habits, which lead to political prosperity, Religion and Morality are indispensable supports.
significance: Washington held that a free society rests on faith and moral character, not only on laws and institutions.

author: George Washington
text: I hold the maxim no less applicable to public than to private affairs, that honesty is always the best policy.
significance: The same honesty expected at home should guide public and professional life; integrity should not change with the setting.

author: George Washington
text: Let us therefore animate and encourage each other, and show the whole world that a Freeman, contending for liberty on his own ground, is superior to any slavish mercenary on earth.
work: General Orders, Headquarters, New York (2 July 1776)
significance: In hard moments, mutual encouragement is itself a form of leadership that strengthens a whole team.

author: Winston Churchill
text: I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat.
work: First speech as Prime Minister, House of Commons (13 May 1940)
significance: Honest leaders tell people the true cost of a hard task; candour builds more trust than false comfort.

author: Winston Churchill
text: Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning.
work: Speech at the Lord Mayor's Luncheon, Mansion House, London (10 November 1942)
significance: An early success is worth marking, but a long effort still lies ahead; perseverance means not mistaking a start for a finish.

author: Winston Churchill
text: The price of greatness is responsibility.
significance: Influence and position bring obligations; the more we are given, the more we are answerable for.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Order. Let all your things have their places; let each part of your business have its time.
work: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
significance: Simple order in our things and our time frees attention for the work and people that matter most.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Sincerity. Use no hurtful deceit; think innocently and justly, and, if you speak, speak accordingly.
work: Autobiography, Part II (list of thirteen virtues, 1784)
significance: Honest speech starts with honest thinking; what we say should match what we truly believe.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: I grew convinc'd that truth, sincerity and integrity in dealings between man and man were of the utmost importance to the felicity of life
significance: Franklin found by experience that trustworthy dealings are central to a happy life, not just a moral rule.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Whenever anything is being accomplished, it is being done, I have learned, by a monomaniac with a mission.
significance: Great work usually needs someone single-minded enough to carry it, which shows the value of focused commitment.

author: Peter Drucker
text: To be a manager requires more than a title, a big office, and other outward symbols of rank. It requires competence and performance of a high order.
significance: Authority is earned through competence and results, not through titles or the trappings of position.

author: Peter Drucker
text: A manager's task is to make the strengths of people effective and their weakness irrelevant - and that applies fully as much to the manager's boss as it applies to the manager's subordinates
significance: Good leaders arrange work around people's strengths, and that generosity applies to their own bosses as well.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: A people that values its privileges above its principles soon loses both.
significance: When comfort is placed above conviction, both are eventually lost, in nations and in families alike.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.
work: Address to the World Council of Churches, Evanston (19 August 1954), quoting a former college president
significance: Urgent demands can crowd out the important ones; wise people protect time for what truly matters.

author: Dwight D. Eisenhower
text: As their heirs, may we never confuse honest dissent with disloyal subversion.
work: Speech at the Columbia University Bicentennial (31 May 1954)
significance: Healthy teams and communities can tell honest disagreement apart from disloyalty, and make room for it.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: No race can prosper till it learns that there is as much dignity in tilling a field as in writing a poem.
work: Up From Slavery, ch. 14, Atlanta Exposition Address (1901)
significance: All honest work carries dignity, whether done with the hands or the mind, and deserves equal respect.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: I have begun everything with the idea that I could succeed, and I never had much patience with the multitudes of people who are always ready to explain why one cannot succeed.
significance: Hopeful determination opens doors that excuses keep shut; beginning with belief matters.

author: Booker T. Washington
text: Perhaps the most valuable thing that I got out of my second year was an understanding of the use and value of the Bible.
significance: A teacher's influence can be lifelong; for Washington, learning to love Scripture was the best fruit of school.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: Power concedes nothing without a demand. It never did and it never will.
work: West India Emancipation speech, Canandaigua, New York (3 August 1857)
significance: Injustice rarely corrects itself; it takes people willing to speak up and press for what is right.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: I felt as I never felt before. It was a glorious resurrection, from the tomb of slavery, to the heaven of freedom.
work: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, ch. 10 (1845)
significance: Standing up to oppression restored Douglass's spirit, showing how courage can renew a person from within.

author: Frederick Douglass
text: Not transient and fitful effort, but patient, enduring, honest, unremitting and indefatigable work, into which the whole heart is put
significance: Success comes less from bursts of effort than from steady, honest work done wholeheartedly over time.

author: John Adams
text: Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passion, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence
work: Argument in defence of the British soldiers, Boston Massacre trials (4 December 1770)
significance: Good decisions start from facts rather than feelings; leaders must let evidence correct their preferences.

author: John Adams
text: I must study Politicks and War that my sons may have liberty to study Mathematicks and Philosophy.
significance: Parents often do hard, unglamorous work so their children can have wider opportunities; sacrifice can be a gift.

author: John Adams
text: Let us tenderly and kindly cherish, therefore, the means of knowledge. Let us dare to read, think, speak, and write.
work: A Dissertation on the Canon and Feudal Law (1765)
significance: Learning is to be cherished and used boldly; a free people needs the courage to read, think and speak.

author: John Adams
text: I pray Heaven to bestow the best of blessings on this house and all that shall hereafter inhabit it. May none but honest and wise men ever rule under this roof.
significance: Written on his first night in the White House, it is a prayer that any home or office be led with honesty and wisdom.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: Whenever you are to do a thing, though it can never be known but to yourself, ask yourself how you would act were all the world looking at you, and act accordingly.
significance: Character is what we do when no one is watching; a simple test is to act as if everyone could see.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: Give up money, give up fame, give up science, give the earth itself and all it contains, rather than do an immoral act.
significance: Written as advice to a teenage nephew, it places integrity above wealth, fame or achievement.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: Encourage all your virtuous dispositions, and exercise them whenever an opportunity arises; being assured that they will gain strength by exercise, as a limb of the body does
significance: Virtues grow with practice like muscles; small daily acts of goodness build habits that last.

author: Thomas Jefferson
text: Honesty is the first chapter in the book of wisdom.
significance: Wisdom starts with honesty; cleverness without truthfulness leads people astray.

author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
text: The great affairs of life are not performed by physical strength, or activity, or nimbleness of body, but by deliberation, character, expression of opinion.
work: On Old Age, ch. 6, trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
significance: Wisdom and character, which can deepen with age, matter more for life's big tasks than speed or strength.

author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
text: Such friendship enhances prosperity, and relieves adversity of its burden by halving and sharing it.
work: On Friendship, ch. 6, trans. E. S. Shuckburgh
significance: True friends double our joys and halve our troubles, which makes investing in friendship worthwhile.

author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
text: We are not born for ourselves alone, but our country claims a share of our being, and our friends a share
work: De Officiis, Book I, §22, trans. Walter Miller (1913)
significance: Our lives are bound up with others; family, friends and community all have a rightful claim on us.

author: Marcus Tullius Cicero
text: The better and more noble, therefore, the character with which a man is endowed, the more does he prefer the life of service to the life of pleasure.
work: De Officiis, Book III, §25, trans. Walter Miller (1913)
significance: Noble character shows itself in choosing service over comfort, a mark of good leaders and parents alike.

author: William Wilberforce
text: God Almighty has set before me two great objects, the suppression of the Slave Trade and the Reformation of Manners.
work: Journal (28 October 1787), in The Life of William Wilberforce (1838)
significance: A clear sense of calling can focus a whole life; Wilberforce pursued these two aims for decades.

author: William Wilberforce
text: Beat the world at its own best weapons. Let your love be more affectionate, your mildness less open to irritation, your diligence more laborious, your activity more wakeful and persevering.
significance: Believers commend their faith best by outdoing others in love, patience and hard work.

author: William Wilberforce
text: Consider sweetness of temper and activity of mind, if they naturally belong to you, as talents of special worth and utility, for which you will have to give account.
significance: Even our temperament is a gift to steward; a kind spirit and an active mind are talents to use well.

author: Ronald Reagan
text: The future doesn't belong to the fainthearted; it belongs to the brave.
work: Address to the Nation on the Challenger Disaster (28 January 1986)
significance: Spoken to grieving schoolchildren, it reminds us that progress needs courage even after painful loss.

author: Ronald Reagan
text: Freedom is never more than one generation away from extinction. We didn't pass it on to our children in the bloodstream.
work: Address to the Phoenix Chamber of Commerce (30 March 1961)
significance: Values are not inherited automatically; each generation must teach them deliberately to the next.

author: Ronald Reagan
text: We have every right to dream heroic dreams. Those who say that we're in a time when there are not heroes, they just don't know where to look.
significance: Everyday heroes are all around us in ordinary jobs and homes, if we learn to notice and honour them.

author: Margaret Thatcher
text: You know, if you just set out to be liked, you would be prepared to compromise on anything, wouldn't you, at any time? And you would achieve nothing!
work: Interview for the Press Association (3 May 1989)
significance: Leaders who need to be liked above all lose their way; doing what is right sometimes costs popularity.

author: Margaret Thatcher
text: I started life with two great advantages: no money, and good parents.
significance: Good parenting can outweigh material advantage; what children receive at home matters more than wealth.

author: Margaret Thatcher
text: Pennies don't fall from heaven, they have to be earned here on earth.
work: Speech at the Lord Mayor's Banquet (12 November 1979)
significance: Provision comes through honest work; resources must be earned and handled with care, not assumed.
